newsitem.title: USA: Clinton budget seeks funds for IMF emergency pool.
newsitem.headline: Clinton budget seeks funds for IMF emergency pool.

text.p: President Clinton's fiscal 1998 budget includes a one-time appropriation of $3.5 billion to provide a financial cushion in the event of an economic crisis that threatens the global monetary system.

The IMF's New Arrangements to Borrow, a recently approved war-chest that the International Monetary Fund can draw on in cases where a country's economic problems are so severe that they may spill over to the entire monetary system, amounts to about $48 billion and includes pledges from 25 countries.

The $3.5 billion U.S. share will not count as an outlay or increase in the deficit as the United States will receive an increase in its international reserve assets that corresponds to any transfer to the IMF under the NAB, the budget said.
The new pool of funds was one result of the Mexican peso crisis that hit suddenly in late 1994 and quickly spread to other emerging economies and at one point seemed to threaten the entire system.

"As the Mexican peso crisis demonstrated, the increase in the interdependence of our trading and monetary system means that a monetary crisis in any major trading nation affects all nations," the Budget said.
The Clinton budget also noted that the administration is in the process of reviewing quotas as part of the IMF's 11th general review of its financial needs.
IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus has said he would like to see the IMF quota, or overall financing, doubled to $440 billion, of which the U.S. share would be about 17 percent.
"A specific amount for any agreed increase in the United States quota resulting from these negotiations will be requested upon their conclusion," the Budget said.
Like the NAB, however, the U.S. share would not be scored as an outlay because the United States receives an increase in its international reserves corresponding to its contribution.
The administration also is seeking $1.03 billion for the World Bank's International Development Association, which assists poor countries by make essentially interest-free credits available.
Of that total, $234.5 million is to clear arrears in unmet U.S. commitments, while the remainder is the U.S. contribution to the 11th replenishment.

The Budget noted that the U.S. will meet this month with other IDA donors to review procurement restrictions placed on the United States because of delays in meeting its commitments and not taking part in an interim arrangement.

Because of U.S. arrears, IDA is being partly financed by an Interim Trust Fund from other donor nations, resulting in U.S. companies being being barred from bidding on contracts financed by the the trust fund.

Some in Congress have criticized the World Bank for the restrictions, threatening to withhold funding for IDA, while the U.S. Treasury has expressed the view that the restictions are counter-productive and should be lifted.
